sections.h2: Who qualifies for the Ohio homestead exemption?
sections.html:
Ohio gives the exemption to owner-occupants who are 65 or older, permanently and totally disabled, or the surviving spouse of someone in those groups. Disabled veterans, their surviving spouses, and surviving spouses of public service officers killed in the line of duty have their own larger reduction. The definitions sit in R.C. 323.151.

Age is counted in a specific way. For this purpose, 'sixty-five years of age or older' means a person who reached 64 before January 1 of the year of application. The Department of Taxation adds that a senior owner must be 65 by December 31 of the year the application is filed.

The home itself has to meet several tests:

  • It is a dwelling the applicant owns and occupies as a home, with Ohio as the domicile.
  • It includes the surrounding land only up to one acre that is reasonably needed for the home.
  • It was not acquired from a relative, other than a spouse, for the purpose of qualifying.
  • An owner can be a life tenant, a vendee in possession under a land contract, a mortgagor, or the settlor of a trust that holds title to a home the settlor occupies.

The Department of Taxation notes that homes held by corporations, partnerships and LLCs generally do not qualify, because the owner is not an individual.

sections.h2: How much does the exemption take off an Ohio tax bill?
sections.html:
It takes the form of a credit on the property tax bill, calculated on a slice of the home's market value. The size of the credit also depends on the local tax rate: the Department of Taxation says that the higher the rate, the higher the credit. The reduction amounts are indexed for inflation each year.

Homestead reduction amounts and income limit printed by the Ohio Department of Taxation (real property)
ItemTax year 2025Tax year 2026
Low-income senior or disabled owner$29,000$29,700
Disabled veteran, or surviving spouse of a public service officer killed in the line of duty$58,000$59,400
Income threshold for seniors and disabled owners$40,000$41,000

Source: Ohio Department of Taxation, Homestead Means Testing FAQ. Income is measured by modified adjusted gross income, which the statute defines for the owner and spouse for the year before the application.

No income test applies to disabled veterans, their surviving spouses, or the surviving spouses of public service officers. Owners who received the exemption in 2013, before means testing returned, are also outside the income test.

sections.h2: Where and when do you file in Ohio?
sections.html:
File with the county auditor of the county where the home sits, on or before December 31 of the year the reduction is sought. The Department of Taxation lists three forms: DTE 105A for most applicants, DTE 105I for disabled veterans and their surviving spouses, and DTE 105K for surviving spouses of public service officers. Every county auditor must take a paper copy, and some accept electronic filing.

A disability claim needs a certificate. R.C. 323.153 calls for a physician's certificate for a physical disability, and a physician or psychologist licensed in Ohio for a mental one. A certificate from a state or federal agency that classifies disability also works. Veterans attach written confirmation from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs.

After filing, the sequence runs like this:

  • The auditor approves or denies the application and sends notice within thirty days of that decision.
  • A denial notice must state the reasons.
  • An owner who thinks the denial was wrong, or the reduction too small, can appeal to the county board of revision within sixty days of the notice, using form DTE 106B.
  • Each January the auditor mails a continuing application. Send it back only if ownership, occupancy, disability or income changed.

A false statement made to get the reduction is a fourth-degree misdemeanor and bars the reduction for three years after a conviction.

sections.h2: What happens to the exemption when an Ohio owner sells?
sections.html:
The reduction follows the owner, not the house. Under R.C. 323.152(C), a transfer of ownership after an application was filed does not forfeit the reduction for that year. Once the home is sold, though, the seller no longer owns or occupies it, so the continuing application should be returned to the auditor reporting the change.

Failure to report has a price. If the auditor or treasurer finds that an owner kept a reduction after losing eligibility, a charge goes on the property for each affected tax year, with interest as if the reduction were delinquent tax. That charge is collected like delinquent taxes, which makes it a closing item for a title company to catch.

The buyer starts from a different place. The partial exemption for homesteads in R.C. 323.152(B)(2) calls for a fresh application when a home changed hands in the preceding year, and the auditor mails an original application each February for homes that transferred. The filing deadline is again December 31. A senior or disabled buyer who moves in must apply at the new address, and the Department of Taxation says to begin in January of the year after the move. Ownership and occupancy as of January 1 decide the tax year.

sections.h2: What other Ohio property tax reductions sit next to the homestead exemption?
sections.html:
Three other pieces of relief show up on Ohio residential bills. The first is the partial exemption under R.C. 319.302, which the auditor reviews parcel by parcel as of January 1. For residential property it is listed at seven and one-half percent for the first tax year the amendment applies, with later steps ending at zero percent for and after the third following tax year. Ask the auditor what percentage applies to a given bill.

The second is the owner-occupancy credit, which the Department of Taxation describes as a reduction on a primary residence occupied on January 1 of the application year. Owners should ask the auditor whether it already appears on their bill.

The third is a county option created by House Bill 96, signed in June 2025. County commissioners may adopt a local-option homestead exemption that mirrors the state one, with the same eligibility rules and the same amount. Nobody applies for it separately: anyone already getting the state exemption receives it automatically once a county turns it on. Whether a given county has done so is a question for the auditor.

Farmland has its own track, the Current Agricultural Use Value program, which also runs through the auditor.

sections.h2: Does the exemption change how an Ohio house sells?
sections.html:
It rarely changes the sale itself, but it affects the tax figures on the settlement statement. A seller who has been receiving the credit should bring the most recent tax bill to the closing, since the credit shows there. A buyer who plans to live in the house should ask the title company how the owner-occupancy filing is handled at the county auditor's conveyance step.

A few practical points for sellers:

  • An heir who inherits a home does not get the seller's reduction automatically. Eligibility depends on the new owner's own age, disability and occupancy.
  • A home under a land contract can still qualify, because R.C. 323.151 counts a vendee in possession as an owner.
  • Pending appeals and unpaid installments are matters for the county treasurer, who bills and collects the tax.

Selling a house with back taxes, a tenant, or heavy repairs is a different problem from the exemption. A direct sale to a cash buyer skips showings and repair negotiations, and the title company still handles any tax proration at closing.

faqs.q: Do I have to reapply for the Ohio homestead exemption every year?
faqs.a: No. Once approved, the application continues for each year the dwelling is your homestead. The auditor mails a continuing application each January, and you return it only if your income, ownership, occupancy or disability status changed.

faqs.q: What is the last day to file the Ohio homestead exemption for real property?
faqs.a: December 31 of the year the reduction is sought. Manufactured and mobile homes taxed that way file by December 31 of the year before. The statute allows a late application for the preceding year to be filed with an original application.

faqs.q: Can I get the Ohio homestead exemption if my home is in a trust?
faqs.a: Often yes. The Department of Taxation says revocable and irrevocable trusts can qualify when the trust gives you complete possession of the property. Check the trust language with the county auditor before applying.

faqs.q: Who decides the Ohio homestead exemption, and where do I appeal?
faqs.a: The county auditor decides it. If you believe the denial or the amount is wrong, file a complaint with the county board of revision within sixty days of the auditor's notice.

faqs.q: Does selling my Ohio home end the exemption?
faqs.a: Yes, for future years. The reduction applies to a home you own and occupy, so tell the auditor when you no longer qualify. Skipping that step can lead to a charge on the property with interest for years the reduction should not have been given.
